intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself with the questions, and write your own notes in the space beside mine.

sections.title: Why method matters
sections.big_idea: Research is a disciplined way of being less wrong: **a careful sceptic could follow every step** from your question to your conclusion.
in_plain_words: Everyday knowing is built from what you happened to see and who you happened to ask, so it is fast and impossible to audit. Research knowing records a stated question, a design chosen in advance, a sample drawn by a rule, tested measures and an analysis anyone can repeat. The process is a chain of six decisions, and a weak early link cannot be repaired later.

Method matters in public life. Official estimates of India's poverty fell from 36 to 26 per cent in the 1990s, and Deaton and Kozel found good evidence the decline was too optimistic. A consumption survey from 2017-18 was never released. Three habits recur throughout: write it down first, look for what would prove you wrong, and claim in proportion.

nodes.label: Question
nodes.sub: what do we need to know?

nodes.label: Write-up
nodes.sub: who needs it, in what form?

diagram.caption: the research process is a chain of decisions

key_terms.meaning: The record of the choices you made on the way to an answer.
Could a careful sceptic follow every step and arrive where you did?
State the question, comparison and analysis before seeing outcome data.
Say a 400-household survey describes that district only.
Part of method: data nobody trusts or can see cannot inform decisions.

worked_example.title: Learn from the poverty numbers
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's two cases to see why method is never a footnote.
steps: Official poverty fell from 36 to 26 per cent between 1993-94 and 1999-2000: 36 − 26 = 10 percentage points.
Deaton and Kozel found no full consensus and good evidence that the official fall was too optimistic, particularly for rural India.
Their issues were questionnaire design, reporting periods and non-response. These are method choices.
The previous published consumption round was 2011-12 and the next was 2022-23: 2022 − 2011 = 11 years without a published distribution.
Apply the sceptic test to your own notes: could someone follow every step?
worked_example.answer: A 10-point headline fall that was contested, and an eleven-year gap. Credibility is part of method.

mistakes: Treating the choice of survey questions as a technical footnote. It became a national political argument.
Repairing a weak sample with a sophisticated regression. A weak early link cannot be repaired later.
Writing the analysis plan after seeing outcomes. A plan written afterwards can always be made to fit.
Generalising from one district to a state. Claim in proportion to the sample.

recall.q: What are the six links in the research chain?
recall.a: Question, design, sample, measures, analysis and write-up.

recall.q: When are mistakes cheapest to fix?
recall.a: At the question and design stage, before fieldwork.

recall.q: What fall in poverty did the official estimates show in the 1990s?
recall.a: From 36 per cent in 1993-94 to 26 per cent in 1999-2000.

recall.q: Which round of the consumption survey was not released, and when was the decision announced?
recall.a: The 75th round (2017-18); MoSPI announced it on 15 November 2019.

recall.q: Name the three habits that separate research from reporting.
recall.a: Write it down first, look for what would prove you wrong, claim in proportion.

sections.title: Framing answerable questions
sections.big_idea: A problem becomes a research question when you can say **what evidence would answer it,** and two people would plan the same study.
in_plain_words: Practitioners arrive with a problem, and research needs a question narrow enough that a specific body of evidence would answer it. Name the population, place, time and quantity of interest. Questions come in three families: descriptive, explanatory and evaluative. Check worth with FINER, and structure evaluative questions with PICO plus setting and time.

Concepts become indicators through an operational definition: which question, asked of whom, coded how, over which period. Hypotheses are predictions that could fail, drawn from a theory of change. Remember whose question it is. Questions set by funders or ministries tend to ask about coverage, cost and targets, and scoping with participants can reveal what they consider the main problem.

diagram.caption: narrowing a problem into an answerable question

key_terms.meaning: Narrow enough that a specific body of evidence would answer it.
Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant.
Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, plus setting and time.
The exact procedure that turns a concept into a recorded value.
No difference; tests ask how surprising the data would be if it were true.

worked_example.title: Narrow a school problem
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's class 8 example to move from problem to question and test it.
steps: Problem: girls in a block stop attending school after class 8.
Topic: the transition to secondary school.
Question: what share of girls who finish class 8 in 2025 enrol in class 9, and how does it vary with distance to the nearest secondary school?
Test: it names population, place, time and quantity, so two people would plan the same study. Its family is descriptive.
A question like 'did the bicycle scheme keep them in school?' is evaluative and needs a comparison.
worked_example.answer: A descriptive question with evidence named: enrolment records plus a household survey with distance measured.

mistakes: Keeping a slogan such as 'improve nutrition' as the question. Turn it into something observable.
Asking an evaluative question with no Comparison row. It is then a descriptive question about participants.
Using a different definition from NFHS or PLFS and then comparing with their figures.
Ignoring who set the question. Questions from above can miss what participants consider the main problem.

recall.q: Name the three question families.
recall.a: Descriptive, explanatory and evaluative.

recall.q: Which FINER letter kills more studies than any other?
recall.a: F, for Feasible.

recall.q: What are the six rows of the PICO table used in the deck?
recall.a: Population, intervention, comparison, outcome, setting and time.

recall.q: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation in the deck's example?
recall.a: 'How many women were trained?' is monitoring; 'Did training change practice?' needs a comparison.

recall.q: Which PLFS frameworks differ in reference period?
recall.a: Usual status (last 365 days) and current weekly status (last seven days).

sections.title: Ways of knowing
sections.big_idea: Every design assumes answers to **what is there to know and how we can know it.** Knowing which ones makes you a better reviewer.
in_plain_words: Ontology asks what is there to know, and epistemology asks what makes a claim credible. They show up as practical choices: a fixed questionnaire or an open interview, a sample to represent or to illuminate. Four traditions bundle these choices: positivist and post-positivist, interpretivist, critical, and pragmatist.

Post-positivism measures imperfectly and answers with procedure, as large statistical systems do. Interpretivism finds the meanings that standard instruments flatten but cannot estimate prevalence. Critical traditions ask who benefits, who is missing and who owns the data. Pragmatists start from the decision. Whatever the tradition, reflexivity means recording how your position affected the research.

children.label: Interpretivist
items: Social reality is made through meaning

diagram.caption: what each tradition assumes and counts as evidence

key_terms.meaning: What is there to know.
How we can know it, and what makes a claim credible.
Noticing and recording how the researcher affects the research.
A short statement in the protocol of who you are relative to participants.
Start from the question and the decision, and pick the mix that serves them.

worked_example.title: Name the tradition
worked_example.setup: Place each illustrative case in one of the four traditions.
steps: A national survey uses standard instruments, trained enumerators, probability samples and weights: post-positivist.
An interview shows a woman recorded as doing 'no work' grazed goats and carried water, and her family does not call it work: interpretivist.
A study builds questions with those affected, and asks who owns the data afterwards: critical.
A programme evaluation combines whatever strands best serve the decision: pragmatist.

mistakes: Treating the traditions as rival camps. Many researchers move between them, sometimes within one study.
Using 'we used what was convenient' as a justification. Pragmatism owes an account of why each method was chosen.
Leaving the researcher out of the account. Interviewer caste and sex can change the conversation.
Treating a large survey as neutral. The critical questions improve any study.

recall.q: Which tradition do NSS, Census and NFHS follow?
recall.a: Post-positivist.

recall.q: What are the limits of interpretive research?
recall.a: Small purposive samples cannot estimate prevalence, and findings depend on the researcher's skill and position.

recall.q: Name two critical-tradition questions.
recall.a: Any two of: who is missing from the frame, whose language, who was in the room, who owns the data, who is an author, who sees results.

recall.q: What is the risk of pragmatism?
recall.a: Shallowness: two weak strands do not make a strong study.

recall.q: What does reflexivity ask you to do in the protocol?
recall.a: Write a positionality note and keep a field diary.

sections.title: Choosing a design
sections.big_idea: The question chooses the design, and **every design has a main threat** you should name in the protocol.
in_plain_words: Start from the question family and let it choose the design. The design table pairs each question with a design family, typical data and its main threat. Description done well is valuable on its own, as ASER shows. Time matters too: cross-section, repeated cross-section or panel, with panels powerful but fragile.

Explanatory designs depend on case selection by a stated rule. Correlation is a clue because a confounder, such as wealth, can create an association. Evaluative designs build a comparison by chance or by a rule, and each rests on an assumption. Four validity questions apply to any finding, and constraints are design inputs to state openly. Shrink the question when the design cannot answer it.

diagram.caption: match the design family to the question family

key_terms.meaning: The same units observed repeatedly.
A factor influencing both exposure and outcome.
Did the exposure cause the outcome?
Do the measures capture the concepts?
Testing each link of the theory of change with mixed evidence.

worked_example.title: Pick a design for four questions
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's table to pick a design family and name the main threat.
steps: 'How many girls are out of school, by district?' Descriptive cross-section. Main threat: frame coverage and non-response.
'How has it changed since 2018?' Repeated cross-section with a stable method. Main threat: changes in method or definitions.
'Why do they leave?' Explanatory: interviews, case studies. Main threat: selective sampling and researcher bias.
'Did a bicycle scheme keep them in school?' Evaluative: compare exposed and unexposed. Main threat: confounding and selection.
worked_example.answer: Cross-section, repeated cross-section, explanatory, evaluative. Each threat goes into the protocol.

mistakes: Starting from a method you like and fitting a question to it.
Concluding that toilets cause growth from taller children in households with toilets. Those households are richer and nearer to services.
Using a repeated cross-section to claim the same households escaped poverty. Only a panel can show that.
Strengthening one validity type without noticing it weakened another.

recall.q: Which design shows whether the same households escaped poverty?
recall.a: A panel.

recall.q: What makes ASER's trends credible?
recall.a: The same tasks and sampling approach each round.

recall.q: What are the four validity types?
recall.a: Statistical conclusion, internal, construct and external.

recall.q: Which design fits a programme already rolled out when randomisation is ruled out?
recall.a: Difference-in-differences or a matched comparison.

recall.q: What is the dangerous move under constraints?
recall.a: Keeping an ambitious question and silently using a design that cannot answer it.

sections.title: Sampling logic
sections.big_idea: Probability samples estimate how common something is; purposive samples find what teaches most. **Match the sample to the claim.**
in_plain_words: The target population is everyone the question is about, the frame is the list you actually draw from, and the gap between them is coverage error. Probability sampling gives each unit a known, non-zero chance and supports statements about a population. Non-probability sampling finds information-rich cases. National surveys use multistage designs: stratify for precision, cluster for cost.

ASER's design is four plain steps. Sample size follows a formula, inflated by a design effect and the response rate. Design changes break series, as the PLFS 2025 redesign shows. Weights correct for unequal selection, and response rates must be reported. Qualitative samples stop at saturation, within each group you compare.

diagram.caption: the claim you want to make decides

key_terms.meaning: The list you actually draw from; anyone missing can never be sampled.
The gap between the population and the frame.
The factor by which clustering inflates the needed sample.
Corrects for unequal chances of selection built into the design.
The point where new interviews stop producing new themes.

worked_example.title: Sample size for a proportion
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's formula n = z² p(1−p) / e² with z = 1.96, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05. The response rate is illustrative.
steps: Denominator: 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025, so n = 0.96 ÷ 0.0025 = 384, which the deck rounds to 385.
Apply the design effect of 2 used for illustration: 385 × 2 = 770.
If 80 per cent respond: 770 ÷ 0.8 = 963 households to approach.
worked_example.answer: About 385 under simple random sampling, 770 with a design effect of 2, and about 963 to approach.

mistakes: Reporting percentages from a convenience sample as if they described a population.
Forgetting who is not on the frame: migrants, people in unrecognised settlements, the homeless.
Comparing results across the January 2025 PLFS redesign as if the series were continuous.
Analysing a stratified national survey without weights.

recall.q: What is coverage error?
recall.a: The gap between the population and the frame.

recall.q: How many households per district does ASER's design give?
recall.a: 600: 30 villages with 20 households each.

recall.q: What does halving the margin of error from 10 to 5 points do to n?
recall.a: It roughly quadruples it, from 97 to 385.

recall.q: How large was the NFHS-5 household sample selected?
recall.a: 664,972 households selected; 636,699 interviewed.

recall.q: Why does a Dalit and Savarna comparison need more interviews?
recall.a: Saturation is needed within each group compared.

sections.title: Measurement: validity and reliability
sections.big_idea: Every measure is a chain from idea to data, and **reliability and validity are separate properties,** both needed.
in_plain_words: A concept becomes a dimension, an indicator, an item and a value, and each link can break. Reliability asks whether a measure gives consistent results; validity asks whether it measures the concept you intend. A measure cannot be more valid than it is reliable, so fix reliability first. Validity comes in face, content, criterion and construct forms, and belongs to a measure used for a purpose in a population.

Reliability is checked by test-retest, inter-rater agreement and internal consistency, and field back-checks catch fabricated interviews. The recall period is part of the measure, and HCES 2022-23 designed out order and fatigue effects. Response errors include recall error, social desirability, acquiescence and proxy reporting. Qualitative work uses credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.

diagram.caption: each link in the chain can break

key_terms.meaning: Whether a measure gives consistent results.
Whether a measure captures the concept you intend.
Asking the same respondents again after a short gap.
A supervisor re-asks a few questions of a random subset of households.
Lincoln and Guba's four qualitative quality criteria.

worked_example.title: Reliable, valid, both or neither
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's dartboard picture for four illustrative measures.
steps: A weighing scale that always reads 2 kg heavy: darts tight but off the bullseye. Reliable but invalid; more data will not help.
A question so ambiguous that answers vary with the enumerator's mood and also miss the concept: neither.
Individual readings scatter around the true value, but averages over many respondents work: valid on average, unreliable.
Tight on the bullseye after careful design, testing and training: reliable and valid.
worked_example.answer: Reliable but invalid, neither, valid but unreliable, both. Fix reliability first.

mistakes: Assuming translation carries validity across. A scale validated in urban Delhi needs fresh checking among Santali speakers.
Treating a very high alpha as proof of quality. It can mean redundant items.
Reading a line of nominal MPCE as real growth across changed reference periods.
Using a long interview with one fixed question order. Items asked late get shorter, less careful answers.

recall.q: Name the four kinds of validity in the deck.
recall.a: Face, content, criterion and construct.

recall.q: Name the three kinds of reliability.
recall.a: Test-retest, inter-rater and internal consistency.

recall.q: How did HCES 2022-23 reduce order effects?
recall.a: It rotated all six orders of three questionnaires, canvassed in three separate monthly visits.

recall.q: Which four response errors does the deck list?
recall.a: Recall error, social desirability, acquiescence and proxy reporting.

recall.q: Who proposed credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability?
recall.a: Lincoln and Guba, in Naturalistic Inquiry (1985).

sections.title: Qualitative, quantitative and mixed
sections.big_idea: Choose by the question, and when you combine strands, **integration is where mixed methods earns its cost.**
in_plain_words: Qualitative work is best at meanings, processes and unexpected factors, with small purposive samples. Quantitative work is best at prevalence, magnitude and change, with large probability samples. The labels describe data and logic more than people. Qualitative designs include ethnography, case study, grounded theory, phenomenology and narrative. Quantitative designs include surveys, experiments, secondary analysis, administrative data and modelling.

Three core mixed designs are convergent, explanatory sequential and exploratory sequential. Running a survey and focus groups in separate chapters is two studies under one cover; integration means building, explaining, merging or embedding. Participatory approaches share control with communities and can be captured by the powerful. The decision table helps choose what to lead with and what to watch for.

children.label: Exploratory sequential
items: Then build or adapt an instrument

key_terms.meaning: Combining qualitative and quantitative strands and integrating them.
Each strand changes what you conclude from the other.
Themes or indicators in rows, with survey and interview findings alongside.
Using different strands to check one another.
Participatory processes taken over by the powerful.

worked_example.title: Choose the mixed design
worked_example.setup: Match each illustrative use to a design from the deck.
steps: A household survey on school costs runs alongside interviews with parents: convergent.
A survey finds one block with low dropout, and interviews then find out why: explanatory sequential.
Interviews first identify local forms of women's work, then survey items are written: exploratory sequential.
In every case, decide the integration point at the protocol stage and budget time for it.

mistakes: Reporting survey and focus groups in separate chapters and calling it mixed methods.
Treating a contradiction between strands as an error. Contradictions are findings.
Drawing a village map in front of the sarpanch and treating it as the whole village.
Squeezing out integration when fieldwork overruns.

recall.q: What does qualitative work do best?
recall.a: Meanings, processes and unexpected factors.

recall.q: What does quantitative work do best?
recall.a: Prevalence, magnitude, comparison and change over time.

recall.q: Who describes the three core mixed designs?
recall.a: Creswell and Plano Clark.

recall.q: Name the four forms of integration.
recall.a: Building, explaining, merging and embedding.

recall.q: When you need to estimate how common something is, what leads?
recall.a: A probability survey.

sections.title: Secondary data in South Asia
sections.big_idea: Check existing data before collecting your own: you **inherit someone else's decisions,** so read the documentation in full.
in_plain_words: South Asia has some of the largest household surveys in the world. India's main sources are NFHS for health, PLFS for employment, HCES for consumption, the Census for a full count and ASER for rural children's learning. Each has quirks: NFHS-5 states were surveyed at different times, PLFS has two activity definitions and a 2025 redesign, and districts change.

Get the data properly: find, sign up, read the questionnaire and sampling appendix, and reproduce one published table before computing anything new. Common errors are ignoring weights or the design, mixing definitions, crossing breaks and treating survey years as calendar years. The Collection of Statistics Act bars identification of informants, and the DPDP research exemption has conditions.

diagram.caption: how to obtain and read microdata properly

key_terms.meaning: Unit-level survey files, distributed after registration.
Activity status over the last 365 days (principal plus subsidiary).
Activity status over the last seven days.
A change in design or definitions that interrupts a series.
Matching an official estimate from the unit-level file.

worked_example.title: Avoid three secondary-data errors
worked_example.setup: You are building a time series of an employment indicator from PLFS and a nutrition indicator from NFHS-5.
steps: Use sampling weights and the design variables, strata and clusters, in every estimate.
Keep usual status and current weekly status apart, and do not mix them across years.
Mark the break between the 2024 and 2025 PLFS designs and avoid reading the step as a labour market change.
Map districts created after March 2017 back to their parents for NFHS-5.
Report the unweighted sample size behind each estimate, and flag very small cells.
worked_example.answer: Weighted, consistent, break marked, geography mapped, and sample sizes reported.

mistakes: Reading 2019-21 as calendar years. It is a fieldwork span.
Computing standard errors without strata and clusters. They come out too small.
Skipping the reproduction test. A mismatch means something is wrong in weights, filters or definitions.
Publishing small-group estimates resting on a handful of cases.

recall.q: Which source covers consumption and inequality?
recall.a: HCES, run by the National Statistics Office.

recall.q: Which survey series has fieldwork that was interrupted by COVID-19?
recall.a: NFHS-5, in its second phase.

recall.q: What does section 9(4) of the Collection of Statistics Act require?
recall.a: Published statistics must not identify any informant, even by elimination.

recall.q: When does the DPDP research exemption take effect?
recall.a: From 13 May 2027, with Rule 16 of the DPDP Rules 2025.

recall.q: What should you log for every download?
recall.a: File name, version, date and source page.

sections.title: Ethics, consent and the law
sections.big_idea: Ethics is part of research design: it decides **whom you may sample, what you may ask,** and what you owe participants afterwards.
in_plain_words: The Belmont Report set three principles, and ICMR 2017 sets four basic principles expanded into twelve general ones. Risk decides review: anonymous or public data are less than minimal risk, routine questioning is minimal, research on children and adolescents is a minor increase, and interventional studies are more than minimal. A researcher cannot decide her own proposal is exempt.

Consent in the field means gatekeepers do not replace individuals, refusal can be silent, autonomy is relational and consent can be a process. Waivers and deception have strict conditions. Privacy law includes Puttaswamy, the DPDP Act and the Collection of Statistics Act. Plan for duty to disclose, participant support and the safety of field teams.

diagram.caption: risk category and likely review, top to bottom

key_terms.meaning: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice.
India's reference guidelines for research ethics in health.
Permission to proceed without individual consent, for low-risk research.
Autonomy understood in relation to social support and equality.
A trait that combined with others points to one person or family.

worked_example.title: Classify four studies by risk
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's table of risk categories and likely review. The committee decides each case.
steps: An analysis of publicly available data: less than minimal risk, likely exemption from review.
Routine questioning of adult respondents: minimal risk, likely expedited review.
Routine research with adolescents, including social and psychological risks: a minor increase over minimal, usually full committee.
A drug or device trial: more than minimal, full committee.
In all four, the researcher submits and the committee decides the review type.
worked_example.answer: Exemption, expedited, usually full committee, full committee, and always the committee's call.

mistakes: Treating community-head permission as individual consent.
Persisting after silence, restlessness or monosyllabic replies. They can be a refusal.
Calling a mystery-client study minimal-review. Deception needs full committee review.
Removing names but leaving caste, occupation and household size together in a small village.

recall.q: How many general principles are in ICMR 2017 Section 1?
recall.a: Twelve.

recall.q: Which section of ICMR 2017 covers social and behavioural sciences research?
recall.a: Section 9.

recall.q: Which case did a nine-judge bench decide on 24 August 2017?
recall.a: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, recognising a fundamental right to privacy.

recall.q: Who decides a proposal is exempt or expedited?
recall.a: The ethics committee, never the researcher (Section 4.8.3).

recall.q: What should the protocol say if sensitive findings are likely?
recall.a: How they will be handled, including disclosure.

sections.title: Analysis plans and pre-registration
sections.big_idea: Decide the analysis before you see the outcomes: **pre-specify what matters most for credibility,** and be open about the rest.
in_plain_words: An analysis plan sets out, before outcome data are examined, how data become answers: outcomes, sample rules, estimation, subgroups and multiple outcomes. The Open Science Collaboration replicated 100 psychology studies and found effects about half the size, and Ioannidis explained why flexible designs and many tests make findings less likely to be true.

Enter studies in the right registry: the AEA RCT Registry, RIDIE, CTRI or OSF. Olken frames pre-analysis plans as a trade-off between credibility and flexibility. Qualitative plans cover the process and leave findings open. Plans change, and the rule is to report deviations openly, label exploratory results, and never present a revised plan as the original.

right.title: Perils
items: Detailed plans can lock in poor choices

key_terms.meaning: How data will become answers, fixed before outcomes are examined.
Depositing a dated plan in a registry before the data arrive.
The main result on which the study is judged.
A change from the plan, reported openly with a reason.
Analysis not planned in advance, labelled as such.

worked_example.title: Respond to a deviation
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's table of situations to choose the response and what to report.
steps: A flood disrupts fieldwork: revise sample or timing, and report the original plan, change, date and reason.
An outcome measure fails in the field: drop or replace it, and report why and the replacement's definition.
A new question emerges from the data: analyse it as exploratory, with a clear label.
A planned model does not converge: use a simpler specification and report both.
A disappointing result: report it as planned, because null results are findings.
worked_example.answer: Every change is allowed if it is reported openly and the plan is never rewritten as if it were original.

mistakes: Writing the plan after the data arrive. A plan written afterwards can always be made to fit.
Hiding a failed outcome measure. Say why it failed.
Over-specifying the plan until sensible adaptations look suspicious.
Skipping a qualitative plan because findings are open. A plan for the process adds credibility.

recall.q: What did the Open Science Collaboration find?
recall.a: Of 100 replications, 36% had significant results, against 97% of the originals, with effects about half the size.

recall.q: Which registry is for impact evaluations in low and middle income countries?
recall.a: RIDIE, run by 3ie.

recall.q: Which registry takes clinical trials in India?
recall.a: CTRI, the Clinical Trials Registry-India.

recall.q: What does the working rule say?
recall.a: Pre-specify what matters most for credibility, and be transparent about everything else.

recall.q: Why do registries keep timestamps?
recall.a: So revisions cannot be presented as the original plan.

sections.title: Putting it to work
sections.big_idea: A sound protocol is **traceable:** every choice on ethics, sampling, measures and analysis leads back to the question.
in_plain_words: Three worked examples follow one case: why girls in three blocks do not move from class 8 to class 9. Existing data confirms and locates the drop but cannot explain it, so the design is explanatory sequential mixed methods. The sample frame is class 8 registers, stratified by block, with about 770 girls per block before non-response, plus purposive interviews until saturation.

Ethics follows from minors being involved: committee review, parental consent plus the girl's assent, and a disclosure protocol. Names are stored separately and deleted after linkage. The analysis plan is registered before endline. A design decision table starts the conversation, the protocol checklist lists the full contents, and realistic timelines warn about ethics review, translation and cleaning.

diagram.caption: from a district problem to a protocol

key_terms.meaning: The living document listing question, design, sample, ethics and analysis.
Every choice can be followed back to the question.
A child's own agreement, given privately beside parental consent.
A secondary-data brief agreed when the full study will be late.
Matching survey answers to school records using names, then deleting the names.

worked_example.title: Size the class 8 study
worked_example.setup: Illustrative figures from the deck's example: three blocks, ±5 points per block, design effect 2.
steps: A ±5 point margin gives 385 under simple random sampling, so with the design effect of 2: 385 × 2 = 770 per block.
Across three blocks: 770 × 3 = 2,310 girls before non-response.
Interviews: 12 to 15 girls who continued and 12 to 15 who did not, which is 12 + 12 = 24 at least and 15 + 15 = 30 at most.
Enrolment is checked against the class 9 enrolment record, because reported enrolment is inflated by social desirability.
Timeline reality check: ethics review alone can take 4 to 12 weeks.
worked_example.answer: About 2,310 girls and 24 to 30 girls interviewed, with the enrolment record as the primary source.

mistakes: Deciding the sample before the question. Every choice should trace back to it.
Underestimating ethics review, translation with pretesting, and data cleaning.
Keeping an ambitious nine-month design when the decision will be taken in four months.
Failing to version and date protocol changes.

recall.q: Why is explanatory sequential mixed methods chosen in the example?
recall.a: Existing data confirms the drop but cannot explain it, so interviews follow the survey.

recall.q: What is the sampling frame in worked example 2?
recall.a: Class 8 registers of government and aided schools, which miss girls who left earlier.

recall.q: What risk category applies because minors are involved?
recall.a: At least a minor increase over minimal risk.

recall.q: Which three stages are most often underestimated?
recall.a: Ethics review, translation with pretesting, and data cleaning.

recall.q: What does a research protocol checklist end with?
recall.a: Timeline, budget and limitations.

sections.title: Writing, dissemination and where next
sections.big_idea: One study, several audiences: **plan each output in the protocol,** and return findings to the people who gave their time.
in_plain_words: A research report follows IMRaD, and reviewers read methods first. A policy brief is two to four pages, leading with the finding and recommendation. Write the report first, then build the brief from it, so the numbers agree. Ministries, partners, participants, funders and researchers each want something different in a different format.

Honest reporting states limitations precisely, treats null results with the same care as positive ones, and follows a reporting guideline such as CONSORT, STROBE, COREQ or PRISMA. Return findings to participants, checking first for harm to a group. Share anonymised data and code with clear access conditions. The closing deck lists ten takeaways and where to go next.

key_terms.meaning: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion.
Two to four pages: finding, recommendation, evidence, limits.
CONSORT, STROBE, COREQ or PRISMA, depending on the study type.
A well-powered finding of no effect, which saves money and redirects effort.
Sharing results with participants in a usable form.

worked_example.title: Match the output to the reader
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's audience table for one study with five readers.
steps: Ministry or department: a brief or short note. Watch for overclaiming certainty.
Implementing partner: a workshop or practical memo. Watch for defensiveness when findings are critical.
Participants and community: a meeting in the local language with a visual summary. Watch for exposing individuals in small groups.
Funder: a report or dashboard. Watch for pressure to frame null results as success.
Researchers: a journal article, working paper or shared data. Watch for long delays.
worked_example.answer: Five readers, five formats, and a different risk for each.

mistakes: Writing the brief and the report separately, so their numbers disagree.
Writing 'small sample' as a limitation. State it precisely.
Presenting one hamlet's low enrolment locally without checking how it could stigmatise families.
Leaving dissemination unbudgeted. It usually does not happen.

notes.2: Twelve sections follow the research process in order, from why method matters through questions, design, sampling and measurement to ethics, plans and writing. Use the slide ranges as a map. Slide 8 later says which other 101 deck holds the depth for each method, so note where you will go next.
notes.4: Everyday knowing is fast and often right, but nobody can audit it. Research knowing records the question, design, sample, measures and analysis so someone else can follow. Use the sceptic test on your own work: **could a careful sceptic, given your notes and data, arrive where you did?**
notes.5: Read the six links as a chain in which an early weak link cannot be repaired later. A brilliant regression on a badly drawn sample answers a question about the wrong people. **Mistakes are cheap at the question and design stage and expensive after fieldwork**, so spend your care early.
notes.6: Two numbers, 36 per cent and 26 per cent, carry a lesson. A design choice in a survey schedule became a national political argument. Deaton and Kozel found no full consensus and good evidence that official estimates of the fall were **too optimistic, particularly for rural India**. Read their issue list as this deck's contents page.
notes.7: A survey run in 2017-18 was never released, and India went eleven years without a published national consumption distribution. Whatever you think of the decision, take the practitioner's lesson: **credibility is part of method.** A dataset nobody trusts or can see cannot inform a decision.
notes.8: This deck is the map and other decks hold the depth. Use the table to route yourself: interviews and coding to Qualitative Methods, questionnaires to Survey Design, causal questions to Impact Evaluation and Causal Inference. **Commission, design or critique with this deck, and go deeper where the table sends you.**
notes.9: Three habits separate research from reporting: write it down first, look for what would prove you wrong, and claim in proportion. A study that could only ever confirm is **a brochure**. Check your own work against each habit, and notice who holds you to each one.
notes.11: Walk the narrowing by hand: problem, topic, question, evidence. A good question names the population, place, time and quantity of interest. **If two people could read it and plan different studies, it is still a topic.** Keep narrowing until they would plan the same one.
notes.12: Name the question family first: descriptive, explanatory or evaluative. Each needs a different design, sample and standard of proof. Watch the trap in the last line: **'How many women were trained?' is monitoring, and 'Did training change practice?' needs a comparison.**
notes.13: Run every draft question through FINER with a colleague who will be honest: Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant. **Feasibility kills more studies than any other letter.** If no decision would change, a question may be interesting and still not worth a field budget.
notes.14: PICO forces precision, and development work adds setting and time. Fill all six rows for your own project. **If you cannot fill the Comparison row, you do not yet have an evaluative question**, only a descriptive one about people who received a programme.
notes.15: Compare the drafts. The 'too broad' and 'too vague' questions fail because each parenthesis hides an unanswered question: which programme, which women, compared with whom. The answerable versions name population, place, comparison and period. **Rewrite a slogan like 'improve nutrition' until it asks about observable things.**
notes.16: An operational definition fixes the question, the respondent, the coding and the reference period. 'Women's work' changes with a 365-day or seven-day window, or with whether unpaid care counts. **Write the definition into the protocol before fieldwork**, and copy NFHS or PLFS definitions exactly if you plan to compare.
notes.17: A hypothesis is a prediction that could fail. State the direction and the reason, name the mechanism, and say what result would count against you. The null says there is no difference, and tests ask how surprising the data would be if it were true. **Build the theory of change first.**
notes.18: Who asked the question shapes what gets found. Questions from above ask about coverage, cost and targets and can miss what participants call the main problem. **Hold scoping conversations with intended participants and frontline workers before fixing the question.** Chambers made the case for putting the last first.
notes.20: Ontology asks what is there to know, and epistemology asks how we can know it. You need not resolve them, but you must know which answers your design assumes silently. They show up as choices such as a fixed questionnaire or an open interview, and **a sample to represent or to illuminate**.
notes.21: Learn the four traditions by what each counts as credible evidence: replicable measurement, detailed accounts of meaning, evidence that exposes inequality, and whatever serves the decision. NSS, Census and NFHS are post-positivist. **Much of what we know about how caste, gender and disability are lived comes from the other three.**
notes.22: Post-positivism measures a reality it admits it measures imperfectly, and answers error with procedure: standard instruments, trained enumerators, probability samples, weights and margins of error. The HCES documents its design in appendices so others can reproduce estimates. **Its discipline is to report error openly.**
notes.23: The Rajasthan example shows interpretivism's value. The survey number is accurate to its definition, and the interview explains why the definition misses her. **Interpretive samples are small and purposive, so they explain mechanisms and cannot estimate prevalence.** The researcher's skill and position must be made visible.
notes.24: Critical traditions treat research as part of the social world it studies. Use the six questions as an audit of any study, including a large survey: who is missing from the frame, whose language, who was in the room, who owns the data, who is an author, who sees results. **These questions improve any study.**
notes.25: Pragmatism starts from the question and the decision. Its risk is shallowness, since two weak strands do not make a strong study, and 'we used what was convenient' gives a reviewer nothing. Reflexivity means noticing that the researcher affects the research. **Write a positionality note and keep a field diary.**
notes.27: Start from the question family and let it choose the design family. The main-threat column is the part to copy into your protocol, because reviewers look for exactly that paragraph. **Name the main threat for your design and say how you will reduce it.**
notes.28: Description is the foundation of most policy. ASER's credibility rests on consistency: the same tasks and sampling each round, so a change in the number is more likely a change in learning than in method. **That consistency is a design decision.** Note the 2024 scale of 605 districts.
notes.29: Match the time design to the question. A cross-section describes now, a repeated cross-section shows how a population changed, and only a panel follows the same units. A repeated cross-section can show that poverty fell, but **only a panel can show whether the same households escaped.** Track attrition.
notes.30: Four explanatory designs answer why and how. Select cases by a stated rule tied to the question, and record why others were not chosen. Correlational analysis is good for generating hypotheses and weak for proving causes. **Explanatory designs live or die on case selection.**
notes.31: Households with toilets have taller children, but they are also richer and nearer to health services. Learn the definitions of confounder and selection, then the four defences. **Control for measured confounders, and admit unmeasured ones remain.** Look for a dose-response pattern and a plausible mechanism.
notes.32: Each evaluative design builds its comparison differently: chance, chance among schools, change over time, or a cut-off. Read the middle column as the sentence you would write in a protocol. **Each design rests on an assumption that cannot be fully tested**, so choose and check it with Impact Evaluation 101.
notes.33: Four validity questions: is the association real, did exposure cause the outcome, do the measures capture the concepts, would it hold elsewhere? **Strengthening one type often costs another.** A tight pilot with high internal validity may say little about a government-run scale-up. Use the table as a reviewer's checklist.
notes.34: Treat constraints as design inputs. Read across each row: what the constraint rules out and a workable alternative. State them in the protocol. **The dangerous move is keeping an ambitious question and using a design that cannot answer it, without saying so.** Shrink the question instead.
notes.36: Learn the vocabulary: population, frame, sample and unit. Coverage error is the gap between population and frame, and anyone missing from the list can never be sampled. The Census 2011 frame is fifteen years old as of October 2026. **Before sampling, ask who is not on the list.**
notes.37: Choose the sampling logic from the claim you want to make. Probability sampling gives each unit a known, non-zero chance, which supports claims like '34 per cent of households in the district'. Non-probability sampling finds information-rich cases. **Twenty interviews at a health centre say nothing about the share of women in the block who use it.**
notes.38: National surveys select villages or urban blocks first, within strata, and then households. HCES 2022-23 grouped households into three categories and selected 18. **Stratify for precision and cluster for cost**: clustering makes each extra household worth less because neighbours resemble each other.
notes.39: ASER's design is four plain steps: district as stratum, 30 villages, 20 households per village, all children. That is 30 × 20 = 600 households per district. **If you cannot describe your sample in four steps, enumerators will not follow it in the field.** Note the trade-off for small subgroups.
notes.40: The formula n = z² p(1−p) / e² gives 385 for p = 0.5 and e = 0.05. Multiply by the design effect and divide by the response rate. The table shows how fast n grows: **halving the margin of error roughly quadruples the sample.** Every subgroup you report separately needs its own adequate sample.
notes.41: The PLFS redesign shows that a design change is a break in the series. From January 2025 first stage units rose from 12,800 to 22,692 and households per unit from 8 to 12. **MoSPI's own note tells users to consider the changes when comparing with earlier publications.** Mark the break.
notes.42: NFHS-5 response rates were high, and men responded less often than women in every state and union territory. Weights correct for unequal chances of selection, and non-response adjustments correct partly for who refused. **Unweighted analysis of a stratified national survey gives wrong national figures.** Always report your response rate.
notes.43: Qualitative samples are chosen for what participants can teach. The usual stopping rule is saturation, when new interviews stop producing new themes. In one study saturation came within twelve of sixty interviews. **Saturation is needed within each group you compare**, which means many more interviews for a Dalit and Savarna comparison.
notes.45: Follow the food insecurity chain from concept to value and ask at each link what could break it: ignored dimensions, translation, the reference period, who answers. **Reliability asks about consistency and validity asks whether you measure the intended concept.** Use an established instrument wherever one exists.
notes.46: Use the dartboard for the four combinations. A scale reading 2 kg heavy is reliable and invalid, and **more data will not help.** The closing logic matters: a measure cannot be more valid than it is reliable, so fix reliability first through clear protocols and training.
notes.47: Four checks on validity: face, content, criterion and construct. Each has a question and a way to check it. **Validity belongs to a measure used for a purpose in a population**, so a scale validated in urban Delhi needs fresh checking among Santali speakers. Translation alone does not carry validity across.
notes.48: Three reliability checks: test-retest, inter-rater and internal consistency. In the field, back-checks are a practical test-retest and catch fabricated interviews. **A very high alpha can mean redundant items** asking the same thing five ways. In qualitative coding, double-code a sample and discuss disagreements.
notes.49: The recall period is part of the measure. The fact sheet notes that earlier rounds used the Mixed Reference Period and later ones the Modified Mixed Reference Period. **Different recall periods for different items produce different totals from the same households.** The chart shows nominal rupees, so it cannot be read as real growth.
notes.50: Two design changes in HCES 2022-23: three questionnaires in all six orders, and three separate monthly visits. Respondents tire, so items asked late get shorter answers. **Rotating the order spreads fatigue evenly and makes it measurable.** The same changes are a reason to take care when comparing with 2011-12.
notes.51: Learn the four response errors with their fixes: recall, social desirability, acquiescence, proxy reporting. Ask sensitive items privately, match interviewer and respondent sex, and interview each person directly. **Pretest with cognitive interviews** and ask respondents what they understood. Record interviewer IDs and check whether answers cluster.
notes.52: Trustworthiness has four criteria, each parallel to a quantitative one: credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability. **Write these practices into the protocol at the start**, because they are hard to reconstruct afterwards. COREQ lists 32 items reviewers use to check interview and focus group reports.
notes.54: Use the table to match approach to question: qualitative for meanings, processes and surprises, quantitative for prevalence, magnitude and change. **The labels describe data and logic more than people.** Good quantitative researchers read transcripts, and good qualitative researchers count when counting helps.
notes.55: Five qualitative designs: ethnography, case study, grounded theory, phenomenology, narrative and life history. Match each to a situation, such as how a ration shop works or turning points like migration. **Data collection methods cut across these designs.** The depth lives in the Qualitative Methods decks.
notes.56: Quantitative designs include surveys, experiments, secondary analysis, administrative data and modelling. Secondary analysis is cheapest per observation and often the most representative. **Administrative data is large and timely but shaped by what officials need to report.** Experiments include randomising question wording.
notes.57: Three core mixed designs differ in timing and purpose. Convergent merges strands, explanatory sequential goes quantitative then qualitative to explain surprising numbers, and exploratory sequential goes qualitative then quantitative to build an instrument. **Decide the design and the integration point at the protocol stage.**
notes.58: Integration means each strand changes what you conclude from the other: building, explaining, merging, embedding. Otherwise it is two studies under one cover. **Contradictions in a joint display are findings**: 80 per cent attending meetings alongside women sitting silent at the back means both are true. Budget time for it.
notes.59: Participatory approaches share control of framing, collecting and interpreting. Tools include mapping, calendars, wealth ranking and scorecards. The caution is capture by the powerful: **a village map drawn in front of the sarpanch may leave out a Dalit hamlet.** Plan facilitation and how disagreement is recorded.
notes.60: Use the decision table as a conversation starter. Find your need in the first column and read across for what to lead with, what to add and what to watch for. When in doubt, ask **which strand the decision-maker will read first**, and make sure it can carry the main answer alone.
notes.62: Check existing data before collecting your own: it saves money, reduces respondent burden and gives you a benchmark. Ask the four questions on the slide. **You inherit someone else's questions, definitions and timing**, so read their documentation in full. Your ethics committee still decides the review type.
notes.63: Use the sources table as a quick reference: NFHS for health and nutrition, PLFS for employment, HCES for consumption, Census for the full count, ASER for rural children's learning. **Read the 'latest round as of October 2026' column** and check for newer releases. MoSPI microdata is at microdata.gov.in.
notes.64: Know three things before using NFHS-5. States were surveyed at different times, some before and some during the pandemic. Districts are those of March 2017. **Use the sampling weights and the design variables in every estimate.** NFHS-6 fact sheets followed in May 2026.
notes.65: PLFS has two definitions of activity status, usual status over 365 days and current weekly status over seven days, plus a history of design changes. **If you build a series across 2024 and 2025, mark the break** and avoid reading the step as a labour market change. Keep the definitions consistent.
notes.66: Cross-country comparison works best with DHS surveys, which share a core questionnaire. Compare the household counts: 30,018 in the Bangladesh DHS, 13,786 in the Nepal DHS, 636,699 for NFHS-5. **Compare with care**, because surveys differ in year, sample and design. NLSS-IV ran for a year to capture seasonal variation.
notes.67: Follow the four steps to get microdata: find, sign up, read, reproduce. **Reproduce one published table exactly before computing anything new.** If you cannot match the official state unemployment rate, something is wrong in your weights, filters or definitions. Log every download with file name, version, date and source page.
notes.68: Seven common errors, all avoidable: ignoring weights, ignoring the design, mixing definitions, crossing breaks, boundary changes, small subgroups and treating survey years as calendar years. **Report the unweighted sample size behind every estimate** and flag estimates that rest on very few cases.
notes.69: Three legal instruments shape secondary data. The Collection of Statistics Act bars identification of informants, even by elimination. Section 11 lets Government disclose schedules for bona fide research with names and addresses deleted. The DPDP research exemption has conditions: **no decision specific to a person, prescribed standards met, and in force from 13 May 2027.**
notes.71: Ethics decides whom you may sample, what you may ask, how you record answers and what you owe participants. Learn the lineage: Belmont's three principles, ICMR 2017's four basic principles expanded into twelve, and the Declaration of Helsinki. **Treat review as part of design**, since it shapes your sample and questions.
notes.72: ICMR 2017 is India's reference. It grew from documents of 1980, 2000 and 2006, and the 2017 edition added social and behavioural sciences research. Its stated scope is research for health, so check your own committee's terms of reference. **Section 9 is the part most development researchers should read in full.**
notes.73: Twelve principles, each with a plain-language check. Read them as pairs in the table and test your protocol against each. **Voluntariness means free choice to join and to withdraw at any time**, and privacy means identity and records are protected. The table paraphrases ICMR Section 1.1.1 to 1.1.12.
notes.74: Risk category decides the type of review. Anonymous or publicly available data are less than minimal risk, routine research on children is a minor increase, and interventional drug or device studies are more than minimal. **A researcher cannot decide that her own proposal is exempt**: all proposals go to the committee.
notes.75: Consent in the field has four lessons: gatekeepers do not replace individuals, read refusal in body language and silence, autonomy can be relational, and consent can be a process. **Permission from a community head comes first, and individual consent is still required.** Never persist when you see signs of refusal.
notes.76: A waiver is possible for less than minimal risk, such as anonymised or public data, and the committee may waive consent for important social research with no more than minimal risk. **Deception needs full committee review**, minimal risk, no alternative and a debrief plan. Mystery-client and audit studies involve deception, so plan the time.
notes.77: Four instruments, one habit: collect only what the question needs. Puttaswamy made privacy a fundamental right, DPDP gives a research exemption from 13 May 2027, the Collection of Statistics Act forbids identification even by elimination, and ICMR asks for storage and anonymisation plans. **Indirect identifiers can re-identify people in small villages.**
notes.78: Three duties sit beside consent: disclosure when you learn of danger, support for participants on sensitive topics, and safety for field teams. **Put the handling of sensitive findings in the protocol before fieldwork.** Safeguarding obligations towards children and vulnerable adults run alongside research ethics.
notes.80: An analysis plan fixes how you turn data into answers before you see outcomes. Use the table as a template: questions, outcomes, sample and data, estimation, subgroups, multiple outcomes and the qualitative strand. **A dated plan shared with a colleague or a registry beats a perfect plan written after the data arrive.**
notes.81: Of 100 replicated psychology studies, 97% of the originals were significant and 36% of the replications were, with effects about half the size. Ioannidis explained why: small studies, flexible designs and many tests lower the chance that a finding is true. **Pre-registration is a cheap protection.**
notes.82: Know where to file. The AEA RCT Registry takes randomised trials, RIDIE takes impact evaluations in low and middle income countries, CTRI takes clinical and health trials in India, and OSF takes any design including qualitative. **ICMR's transparency principle asks that plans and outcomes be made public** while protecting privacy.
notes.83: Olken frames pre-analysis plans as a trade-off. The promises are credibility, discipline and clarity. The perils are that plans cannot anticipate everything and over-detailed ones lock in poor choices. **Pre-specify what matters most for credibility, and be transparent about everything else.** Label exploratory work as exploratory.
notes.84: A qualitative plan sets out the process of analysis and leaves the findings open. Cover transcripts and translation, how coding starts, who codes, how themes link back to the questions, and how negative cases are sought. **Use the Bhojpuri entry as a template** for your own plan.
notes.85: Plans change, and the rule is to change them openly. The table pairs each situation with an acceptable response and what to report. **Never revise the plan after seeing results and present the revision as the original.** A disappointing result is reported as planned, because null results are findings.
notes.87: Walk the example in order: check existing data, split the question, choose a design. Existing data confirms the drop and locates it but cannot explain it, which is why the design is explanatory sequential. **The design follows the decision** the officer can act on: distance, safety or marriage pressure.
notes.88: Work the sample figures. The frame of class 8 registers misses girls who left earlier, so say so. A margin of ±5 points with a design effect of 2 gives about 770 per block, matching the sample-size table. **Each measure names its validity risk**: reported enrolment is inflated by social desirability, so the class 9 enrolment record is primary.
notes.89: Trace every choice back to the question on the first slide of the example. Minors mean at least a minor increase over minimal risk, so go to an ethics committee and obtain parental consent plus the girl's assent. **Store names separately from answers and delete them after linkage.** Registration costs nothing.
notes.90: Start a conversation with this one-page table, then work the choice through the question, the Section 4 threats and your constraints. Read each row across: situation, design, sample, ethics flag. **The ethics flag column reminds you that every design carries one.**
notes.91: Use the checklist for a complete protocol. Ethics committees, funders and journals each ask for most of it, so write it once, well. **A protocol is a living document**: version and date every change, and keep the approved version with your ethics correspondence.
notes.92: The timelines are illustrative, but the lesson is real: teams most often underestimate ethics review, translation with pretesting, and data cleaning. **If the decision will be taken in four months, a nine-month study cannot inform it.** Shrink the study or agree an interim product such as a secondary-data brief.
notes.94: Use IMRaD for the report and a two-to-four-page brief for decision-makers. Reviewers read methods first, so include response rates, deviations and how saturation was judged. **Write the report first, then build the brief from it, so the numbers agree.** Lead the brief with the finding and recommendation.
notes.95: One study has several audiences, each with its own want, format and risk. Fill in the table for your study at the protocol stage. **Dissemination that is unbudgeted usually does not happen.** Watch the funder row: pressure to frame null results as success is a known risk.
notes.96: State limitations precisely: twenty interviews in two villages of one block, all in Hindi, so Santali-speaking households are not represented. **Null results deserve the same care as positive ones.** Use CONSORT, STROBE, COREQ or PRISMA as the study type requires, and report so a systematic review can include you fairly.
notes.97: Plan a return visit: a village meeting, a pictorial summary, a session with frontline workers. **People who gave their time should hear what it produced.** Check how findings could stigmatise a hamlet before presenting locally. When sharing data, remove direct and indirect identifiers.
notes.98: Ten takeaways, each tied to a section. Use them as a closing self-test: can you apply each to your next study? The last line is the thesis: **method is how others come to trust your answer.** Every section was one more way of making the steps visible.
notes.99: This deck walked the whole process once, and the groups here go deeper into each part. Choose by the gap you felt. The suggested path for a new evaluator is Theory of Change, Survey Design, Qualitative Methods, Impact Evaluation, then Research Ethics. **Follow that order if you are new.**
